A judicial body under the Supreme Court
A constitutional authority under the Ministry of Home Affairs
30.x: I4C is an executive framework and is not a statutory body.
30.tq: Test the distinction between statutory and executive institutions.

30.s: I4C was upgraded to an Attached Office in which year?
30.x: I4C was upgraded to an Attached Office in 2024.
30.tq: Discriminate between the years of operationalisation and institutional upgrading.

30.s: The headquarters of I4C is located at:
30.x: The headquarters of I4C is in New Delhi.
30.tq: Use location-based recall for a national institution.

30.s: Which I4C component is intended for reporting all cyber crimes, particularly crimes against women and children?
30.x: The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, cybercrime.gov.in, is used for reporting cyber crimes, especially those against women and children.
30.tq: Match the component with its distinctive operational role.

30.s: The helpline number 1930 is primarily associated with:
o: Training police officers in cyber forensics
Reporting cyber crimes against children only
Reporting financial fraud and initiating rapid freezing of funds
30.x: The 1930 helpline is used to report financial fraud, particularly for action during the ‘golden hour’ to freeze funds.
30.tq: Use a number-to-function association.

30.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?

a. CFCFRMS — Real-time freezing of defrauded funds
b. NCAP — Takedown notices to intermediaries
c. SAHYOG — AI and Big Data crime analytics
d. Samanvaya — Online training of judges
30.x: CFCFRMS facilitates real-time freezing of defrauded funds. NCAP undertakes AI and Big Data crime analytics, SAHYOG issues takedown notices, and CyTrain provides online training to police, prosecutors and judges.
30.tq: Start from the sure component-role pair and reject swapped functions.

30.s: Samanvaya, an I4C platform, is primarily associated with:
o: Freezing bank accounts without any complaint
Issuing digital certificates to government departments
Inter-state cybercrime data sharing and joint investigation support
30.x: Samanvaya supports inter-state cybercrime data sharing and joint investigation.
30.tq: Distinguish the inter-state coordination platform from financial-fraud tools.

30.s: SAHYOG is associated with which function?
o: Freezing defrauded funds in real time
Reporting crimes against women and children
30.x: SAHYOG is used for issuing takedown notices to intermediaries.
30.tq: Test the precise action associated with a similarly themed cyber platform.

30.s: NCAP under I4C is related to:
o: Cybersecurity audits of private companies only
AI and Big Data-based crime analytics
30.x: NCAP is associated with AI and Big Data crime analytics.
30.tq: Break the acronym-function association rather than relying on general cyber terminology.

30.s:
Which one of the following is correctly matched?

a. CyTrain — Online training for police, prosecutors and judges
b. Cybercrime Forensic Lab Consortium — Financial-fraud helpline
c. CFCFRMS — Cybercrime data-sharing platform
 d. National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal — Takedown notices to intermediaries
30.x: CyTrain provides online training for police, prosecutors and judges. The other functions are associated respectively with the Cybercrime Forensic Lab Consortium, CFCFRMS, Samanvaya and SAHYOG.
30.tq: Find the one correctly paired role when several I4C functions are deliberately swapped.

30.s: Which of the following statements is correct regarding Cyber Commandos?
o: They are private ethical-hacking teams appointed by banks.
They are specially trained police cyber units under I4C.
They are military units under the Ministry of Defence only.
They are judicial officers attached to cyber courts.
30.x: Cyber Commandos are specially trained police cyber units functioning under I4C.
30.tq: Reject the authority-swapping trap in an institutional description.

30.s: Under the CFCFRMS Standard Operating Procedure of January 2026, banks may refund frauds below which amount without a court order?
30.x: The January 2026 CFCFRMS SOP permits banks to refund frauds below ₹50,000 without a court order.
30.tq: Use exact-figure recall and distinguish the threshold from nearby amounts.

30.s: Under the CFCFRMS procedure, frozen funds are to be released within 90 days in the absence of orders. The statement is:
30.x: Frozen funds are to be released within 90 days when no contrary orders are received.
30.tq: Test the exact procedural time limit.

30.s:
Which of the following correctly reflects the August 2026 status of selected cybercrime initiatives?
1. The Money Restoration Portal involved 57 banks.
2. The portal covered 36,290 cases and ₹18.05 crore.
3. e-Zero FIR was functional in 19 States.
4. All States had notified Cyber Crime Coordination Centres.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: The Money Restoration Portal involved 57 banks, 36,290 cases and ₹18.05 crore, while e-Zero FIR was functional in 19 States. Only 14 States had notified Cyber Crime Coordination Centres, so statement 4 is false.
30.tq: Spot the absolute statement that reverses a stated partial-coverage figure.

30.s: Which institution is associated with implementing the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy, 2017?
30.x: APTS implements the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy, 2017.
30.tq: Use the implementing-agency trap by separating State and national institutions.

30.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated function or achievement of APTS in Andhra Pradesh cyber security?
o: Auditing Government of Andhra Pradesh applications
Serving as the national headquarters of I4C
30.x: APTS undertakes capacity building, supports critical-infrastructure security through APCSOC and audits government applications. It is not the national headquarters of I4C.
30.tq: Find the institutionally misplaced function.

30.s: The Cybercrime Coordination Centre inaugurated at Krishnalanka Police Station is located in:
30.x: The centre was inaugurated at Krishnalanka Police Station in Vijayawada.
30.tq: Test a specific location associated with a State cybercrime initiative.

30.s: Which of the following was associated with the Cybercrime Coordination Centre at Krishnalanka Police Station?
o: A national cyber tribunal and a CERT-In headquarters
A blockchain court and a digital university
A satellite launch centre and a data embassy
A cyber radar wing and a laboratory
30.x: The centre included a cyber radar wing and a laboratory; plans also included a cyber war room and cyber guard policy.
30.tq: Match a local cybercrime centre with its distinctive facilities.

30.s: The proposed staffing plan for cyber constables in Andhra Pradesh envisaged:
30.x: The plan envisaged 20 cyber constables per district.
30.tq: Recall the exact district-level staffing target.

30.s: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act primarily for violating:
30.x: The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A for violating freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a), and held that it was not saved by Article 19(2).
30.tq: Match the judicial decision with the constitutional provision directly involved.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the decision in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India:
1. Section 66A was struck down.
2. Section 79 was read down.
3. Section 69A was upheld.
4. Section 66A was held to be saved by Article 19(2).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: The Court struck down Section 66A, read down Section 79 and upheld Section 69A. Section 66A was not saved by Article 19(2), making statement 4 false.
30.tq: Separate the provisions struck down, read down and upheld; reject the reversed constitutional conclusion.

30.s: The Budapest Convention on cybercrime was adopted under the auspices of the:
30.x: The Budapest Convention is associated with the Council of Europe.
30.tq: Apply the international-organisation substitution trap.

30.s: Which of the following countries were identified as not being signatories to the Budapest Convention?
o: China, Germany and the United Kingdom
30.x: India, Russia and China were identified as non-signatories to the Budapest Convention.
30.tq: Test membership through a confusable country grouping.

30.s: According to the Global Cybersecurity Index 2024, India was placed in which tier and received what score?
30.x: The Global Cybersecurity Index 2024 placed India in Tier 1 with a score of 98.49.
30.tq: Keep the ranking tier and numerical score together to avoid partial matching.

30.s:
Which of the following correctly represents the current cybercrime-related figures stated for India?
1. e-Zero FIR is functional in 19 States.
2. Only 14 States have notified State Cyber Crime Coordination Centres.
3. CERT-In incidents reached 29.44 lakh in 2025.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: e-Zero FIR was functional in 19 States, only 14 States had notified State Cyber Crime Coordination Centres, and CERT-In incidents reached 29.44 lakh in 2025.
30.tq: Check each current figure independently before selecting the combined option.

30.s: The Supreme Court’s August 2026 direction concerning digital-arrest scams related to:
o: Making the Budapest Convention binding in India
30.x: The Supreme Court directed the formulation of standard operating procedures concerning digital-arrest scams.
30.tq: Match the judicial intervention with its immediate administrative outcome.

30.s: Which criticism has been made regarding the Information Technology Act in the context of emerging cyber threats?
o: It contains no provision relating to electronic records.
It abolishes all government takedown powers.
It lacks provisions specifically addressing AI impersonation and virtual-arrest threats.
30.x: A criticism is that the IT Act lacks specific provisions for AI impersonation and virtual-arrest threats.
30.tq: Distinguish a stated legislative gap from exaggerated absolute claims.

30.s: The debate surrounding the three-hour takedown rule and MHA notices primarily concerns the balance between:
o: Surveillance and takedown powers on one side and free speech on the other
30.x: The debate concerns surveillance and takedown powers versus free speech, with the wider discussion also linked to Section 66A, Section 69A and VPN regulation.
30.tq: Identify the competing constitutional and regulatory interests in a policy debate.

30.s: Which organisation is associated with Cyber Jagrookta Diwas?
30.x: CERT-In is the organisation associated with Cyber Jagrookta Diwas.
30.tq: Use organiser–campaign pairing and reject sectoral regulators or defence agencies.

30.s: Safer Internet Day is observed on
o: the Tuesday of the first week of February
the first Wednesday of every month
30.x: Safer Internet Day is observed on the Tuesday of the first week of February.
30.tq: Distinguish similar cyber-awareness observances by their exact calendar description.

30.s: Cyber Surakshit Bharat is a MeitY initiative launched in 2018 primarily to
o: train CISOs and front-line IT officials of government bodies with industry partners
conduct elections through secure digital platforms
provide military training exclusively to the Armed Forces
30.x: Cyber Surakshit Bharat was launched by MeitY in 2018 with industry partners to train CISOs and front-line IT officials of government bodies.
30.tq: Link the initiative to its target beneficiaries and implementing partnership instead of its broad cyber theme alone.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. ITSSO tracks the time-bound investigation of sexual-offence cases.
2. The Cyber Crime Reporting Portal facilitates online complaints, particularly relating to crimes against women and children.
3. The helpline associated with cybercrime reporting is 1930.
4. ERSS provides the single emergency number 112.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: All four statements are correct. ITSSO tracks sexual-offence investigations, the cybercrime portal accepts online complaints, 1930 is the cybercrime helpline and ERSS uses 112.
30.tq: Group related digital safety services but test their distinct functions and numbers.

30.s: Under the MHA Standard Operating Procedure for CFCFRMS, banks may refund certain fraud losses without court approval when the amount is below:
30.x: Banks may refund frauds below Rs 50,000 without court approval under the stated procedure.
30.tq: Select the threshold value and reject figures borrowed from other fraud cases.

30.s: Cyber Swachhta Kendra, associated with CERT-In, provides:
o: Private keys for all digital signatures
30.x: Cyber Swachhta Kendra provides free tools for cleaning botnets and malware from devices.
30.tq: Identify the service offered by the correct security body.

30.s: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is associated with offensive messages. What is its present legal position as stated in the material?
o: It was transferred to Section 69A in 2015.
It was made applicable only to government networks in 2015.
30.x: Section 66A, which dealt with offensive messages, was struck down in 2015.
30.tq: Test the legal-status change rather than merely the section subject.

30.s: Section 67A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 deals with:
o: Blocking public access to online content
Sexually explicit material in electronic form
30.x: Section 67A concerns sexually explicit material, while Section 67 concerns obscene material more generally.
30.tq: Distinguish the two closely related provisions dealing with obscene and sexually explicit material.

30.s: Which of the following provisions is correctly matched with its subject?
o: Section 69A — Blocking public access to online content
30.x: Section 69A concerns blocking public access to online content. Section 70 concerns protected systems, Section 79 intermediary safe harbour and Section 79A the Examiner of Electronic Evidence.
30.tq: Use elimination among adjacent section numbers and their distinct functions.

30.s: In the context of Andhra Pradesh cyber security institutions, which organisation holds the distinction of being the first CERT-In-empanelled organisation in the State?
30.x: APTS is the first CERT-In-empanelled organisation in Andhra Pradesh and is also identified as the first CERT-In-empanelled auditor in the State.
30.tq: Use the FIRST/LAST cue to identify the uniquely designated organisation.

30.s: CERT-In incidents reached approximately what level in 2025, described as a five-year high?
30.x: CERT-In recorded 29.44 lakh incidents in 2025, described as a five-year high.
30.tq: Place-value discrimination among closely related numerical options.

30.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy
B. ITU Global Cybersecurity Index edition in which India was ranked 10th
C. ITU Global Cybersecurity Index edition in which India was placed in Tier-1
D. CERT-In incidents reaching a five-year high of 29.44 lakh

Select the correct sequence.
30.x: The chronological order is Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy 2017, GCI 2020, GCI 2024, and the CERT-In incident figure for 2025.
30.tq: Use the years attached to the policy, GCI editions and incident data; first and last items fix the sequence.

31.s:
The National Cyber Security Policy, 2013 aimed at which of the following?
1. Securing and developing resilient cyberspace
2. Creating a trained cyber security workforce
3. Promoting research and development and indigenous security technology
4. Establishing an Information Security Assurance Framework
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The policy aimed at resilient cyberspace, trained manpower, research and development, indigenous security technology and an Information Security Assurance Framework.
31.tq: Use the all-inclusive option after checking each policy objective separately.

31.s: The manpower target under the National Cyber Security Policy, 2013 was to create how many cyber security professionals in five years?
31.x: The target was to develop 5 lakh cyber security professionals within five years.
31.tq: Test the exact policy target rather than the broader objective.

31.s: Which of the following followed the National Cyber Security Policy, 2013?
o: A draft National Cyber Security Strategy
31.x: A draft National Cyber Security Strategy followed the 2013 policy; some descriptions refer to it as an updated NCSP 2020.
31.tq: Use sequence and institutional continuity to identify the subsequent strategy.

31.s: The National Cyber Security Policy was released in 2013 by which Union Ministry?
o: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
31.x: The National Cyber Security Policy 2013 was released by the Information Technology Ministry, now known as MeitY.
31.tq: Use the ministry-ownership trap by distinguishing MeitY from neighbouring ministries.

31.s: The vision of the National Cyber Security Policy 2013 is to ensure
o: exclusive protection of military communication networks
a secure and resilient cyberspace for citizens, businesses and government
a fully government-controlled internet exclusively for public institutions
complete elimination of all cybercrime within five years
31.x: The policy envisions a secure and resilient cyberspace for citizens, businesses and government.
31.tq: Identify the precise wording of the policy vision rather than an extreme or exclusive formulation.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT an objective of the National Cyber Security Policy 2013?
o: Replacing all private cyber security institutions with government agencies
Promoting public-private partnership and research and development
31.x: The policy promotes public-private partnership, research and development, infrastructure protection and data security. It does not seek to replace all private cyber security institutions.
31.tq: Find the option that introduces an extreme and unsupported institutional replacement.

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the National Cyber Security Policy 2013:
1. It seeks to promote indigenous security technology.
2. It provides for conformity assessment with incentives.
3. It envisages an Information Security Assurance Framework.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: All three statements describe elements associated with the policy: indigenous security technology, incentivised conformity assessment and an Information Security Assurance Framework.
31.tq: Check each policy component separately before selecting the combination containing all correct statements.

31.s: Which organisation is the nodal agency for incident response and crisis management in India?
31.x: CERT-In is the nodal agency for cyber incident response and crisis management. NCIIPC is associated with the protection of critical information infrastructure.
31.tq: Discriminate between CERT-In’s incident-response role and NCIIPC’s critical-infrastructure role.

31.s: With reference to the National Cyber Security Policy 2013 and the proposed national cyber security strategy, which one of the following is correct?
o: The draft strategy was notified as the operative national policy in 2020.
The 2013 policy was withdrawn immediately after the draft strategy was prepared.
The 2013 policy remains operative, while the proposed 2020 strategy document was not released as a notified policy.
Both documents were formally notified together in 2020.
31.x: The 2013 policy remains the operative policy. The document sometimes referred to as the 2020 policy was a draft strategy and was not released as a notified policy.
31.tq: Separate an operative policy from a draft document by focusing on notification status.

31.s: The draft National Cyber Security Strategy was prepared under the coordination of the
31.x: The draft National Cyber Security Strategy was prepared under the National Cyber Security Coordinator.
31.tq: Apply the ‘who prepared or coordinated it?’ method to distinguish the responsible authority.

31.s: The status of the draft National Cyber Security Strategy is best described as
31.x: The draft strategy remains pending and has not been notified.
31.tq: Use status words carefully; ‘proposed’ and ‘pending’ do not mean notified or implemented.

31.s: The Cyber Crisis Management Plan is a MeitY framework for countering
31.x: The Cyber Crisis Management Plan is a MeitY framework for countering cyber attacks and cyber terrorism.
31.tq: Identify the precise scope of the framework instead of narrowing it to one sector or victim group.

31.s: The Cyber Crisis Management Plan is implemented by
31.x: The Cyber Crisis Management Plan is implemented by all Central and State Governments.
31.tq: Watch for the ‘only’ trap in statements about the coverage of a national framework.

31.s: By July 2025, CERT-In had conducted how many Cyber Crisis Management Plan workshops?
31.x: CERT-In had conducted 205 Cyber Crisis Management Plan workshops by July 2025.
31.tq: Distinguish the workshop count from the separate Cyber Shakti training figures.

31.s: Every ministry, department and organisation is required to designate a
31.x: Every ministry, department and organisation must designate a Chief Information Security Officer, or CISO.
31.tq: Apply the institutional-designation rule to the authority responsible for information security.

31.s: The National Cyber Coordination Centre primarily facilitates
31.x: NCCC supports situational awareness and timely information-sharing in the cyber domain.
31.tq: Match the body with its operational function rather than with a general security label.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly states the outlay and laboratory coverage of the CCPWC scheme?
o: Rs 132.93 crore and cyber forensic-cum-training laboratories in 33 States/UTs
Rs 205 crore and laboratories in all 36 States/UTs
Rs 18.05 crore and laboratories in 13 States/UTs
Rs 53 crore and laboratories in 24 States/UTs
31.x: The CCPWC scheme has an outlay of Rs 132.93 crore and provides cyber forensic-cum-training laboratories in 33 States and Union Territories.
31.tq: Pair the financial figure with its geographical coverage; avoid mixing it with figures from other cyber programmes.

31.s: Under the CCPWC scheme, more than how many personnel had been trained in digital forensics and investigation?
31.x: More than 24,600 personnel had been trained in digital forensics and investigation under the CCPWC scheme.
31.tq: Separate personnel-trained figures from case counts and monetary amounts appearing in related cyber initiatives.

31.s: The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, in the context of the CCPWC scheme, is linked particularly with complaints relating to
31.x: The portal is linked with reporting complaints involving women and children. The scheme is also linked with cyber-safety projects under the Nirbhaya Fund.
31.tq: Identify the intended beneficiary group rather than assuming that every cyber portal has a general or sector-specific mandate.

31.s: Which of the following correctly describes the Cyber Shakti training figures?
o: 305 beginner offline trainees and 53 advanced online trainees
53 beginner online trainees and 305 advanced offline trainees
205 beginner offline trainees and 105 advanced online trainees
305 beginner online trainees and 53 advanced offline trainees
31.x: Cyber Shakti trained 305 women government officials at the beginner online level and 53 at the advanced offline level.
31.tq: Keep both the numbers and the online/offline level labels aligned; they are deliberately easy to reverse.

31.s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
o: RBI Cyber Security Framework for banks — 2016
CERT-In sectoral CSIRT guidelines — only for foreign companies
31.x: The RBI Cyber Security Framework for banks dates to 2016. SEBI’s CSCRF is from 2024, power-sector CERTs operate under the Ministry of Power, and CERT-In guidelines concern sectoral CSIRTs.
31.tq: Start with the sure date–framework pair and eliminate options with swapped years, ministries or scope.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT a stated cyber-security requirement for Urban Co-operative Banks under the RBI framework?
o: Reporting cyber attacks only after approval from SEBI
31.x: Urban Co-operative Banks are required to have a dedicated cyber team, a board-approved policy, MFA, an incident plan and to report all cyber attacks to RBI. SEBI approval is not the stated requirement.
31.tq: Find the wrong authority in a regulatory-compliance statement by asking which regulator has jurisdiction.

31.s: The SEBI Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework (CSCRF) for regulated entities was introduced in
31.x: SEBI’s Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework for regulated entities dates to 2024.
31.tq: Distinguish the SEBI framework’s year from the RBI banking framework’s earlier year.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the power-sector sectoral CERTs under the Ministry of Power?
31.x: The power sector has CERT-Thermal, CERT-Hydro, CERT-Transmission and CERT-Distribution. CERT-Banking is not one of these power-sector CERTs.
31.tq: Use the common sector label to identify the item belonging to a different sector.

31.s: The MeitY Digital Threat Report 2025–26 for BFSI provides a roadmap extending over
31.x: The second edition of the MeitY Digital Threat Report 2025–26 provides an 18-month roadmap towards continuous cyber resilience for BFSI.
31.tq: Read the duration as a roadmap period and avoid substituting a familiar one-year cycle.

31.s: Under the January 2026 CFCFRMS SOP, frozen funds are to be released within
31.x: The SOP provides for release of frozen funds within 90 days.
31.tq: Test the prescribed time limit directly and avoid confusing it with the roadmap period.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the RBI Innovation Hub–I4C arrangement?
o: A cyber insurance agreement signed on 11 January 2026
A data-sharing MoU signed on 11 May 2026
A banking merger agreement signed on 5 August 2026
A data localisation order issued on 16 July 2026
31.x: RBI Innovation Hub and I4C signed a data-sharing Memorandum of Understanding on 11 May 2026.
31.tq: Match the two institutions with the nature and date of their agreement.

31.s: The Money Restoration portal was associated with which of the following figures?
o: 57 banks, all 36 States/UTs, 36,290 cases and Rs 18.05 crore
205 banks, 90 States/UTs, 1,500 cases and Rs 50,000 crore
13 banks, all 28 States, 18,050 cases and Rs 5 crore
33 banks, 24 States/UTs, 24,600 cases and Rs 132.93 crore
31.x: The Money Restoration portal covered 57 banks and all 36 States/UTs, involving 36,290 cases and Rs 18.05 crore.
31.tq: Keep the count of institutions, geographical coverage, cases and amount together as one composite data set.

31.s: Which division of the Ministry of External Affairs is the nodal point for cyber security, data protection, cybercrime and internet governance?
31.x: The Cyber Diplomacy Division of the MEA is the nodal point for these cyber-related international matters.
31.tq: Match the specialised MEA division with the cluster of functions it handles.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. India is part of the Asia-Pacific CERT.
2. India and the United States have a Memorandum of Understanding on cybercrime investigation.
3. The Cyber Diplomacy Division is located in the Ministry of Home Affairs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Cyber Diplomacy Division is a division of the Ministry of External Affairs.
31.tq: Check both membership and agreement facts, then catch the swapped-ministry trap in statement 3.

31.s: APCERT is a coalition of CSIRTs from how many economies?
31.x: APCERT is a coalition of Computer Security Incident Response Teams from 13 economies.
31.tq: Separate the coalition’s membership count from the number of States/UTs in other cyber programmes.

31.s: The first APCERT conference was held in
31.x: The first APCERT conference was held in Tokyo in March 2002.
31.tq: Combine the event’s first occurrence with both its place and date to avoid partial matching.

31.s: Which one of the following is NOT a member of the Colombo Security Conclave as listed?
31.x: The listed members are India, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Maldives, Bangladesh and Seychelles. Nepal is not included in that list.
31.tq: Test membership by comparing every option against the stated group composition.

31.s: Cyber security is one of how many pillars of the Colombo Security Conclave?
31.x: Cyber security is one of the five pillars of the Colombo Security Conclave.
31.tq: Use the exact pillar count and avoid substituting the number of member countries.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about India’s international cyber cooperation:
1. India is a member of the US-led Counter Ransomware Initiative.
2. India participates in the Quad Senior Cyber Group and cybersecurity partnership.
3. Faster CERT-In agreements with foreign counterparts have been urged to address cross-border threats.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: All three statements are correct. India participates in the Quad cyber mechanisms, is a member of the US-led Counter Ransomware Initiative and has been urged to conclude faster CERT-In agreements with foreign counterparts.
31.tq: Group the related cooperation mechanisms and verify that each statement describes a distinct international cyber measure.

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's performance in the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024:
1. India received a score of 98.49.
2. India was assessed as strong in all five pillars of cybersecurity.
3. India was assigned a numerical rank instead of a tier.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: India received a score of 98.49 and was strong in all five pillars. Statement 3 is false because the 2024 Index uses tiers instead of numerical ranks.
31.tq: Find the false statement by distinguishing the current tier system from the earlier ranking system.

31.s: India was ranked 10th in which edition of the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index?
31.x: India was ranked 10th in the GCI 2020. The GCI 2024 shifted from numerical ranks to tiers.
31.tq: Numerical-year discrimination between the earlier rank-based edition and the later tier-based edition.

31.s: ISEA, associated with cybersecurity awareness and capacity building in India, stands for:
31.x: ISEA stands for Information Security Education and Awareness.
31.tq: Direct recall of the expansion of a commonly confusable cybersecurity acronym.

31.s: Which Union Ministry is associated with the ISEA capacity-building project?
o: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
31.x: ISEA is a capacity-building project of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY).
31.tq: Who-would-do-this-job method for identifying the responsible ministry.

31.s:
With reference to CERT-In's workforce-development activities in 2024, consider the following statements:
1. It trained 12,014 IT professionals.
2. The training was conducted through 23 training programmes.
3. The training was conducted by the NM-ICPS.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: CERT-In trained 12,014 IT professionals through 23 trainings in 2024. Statement 3 is false; NM-ICPS supports cybersecurity and AI research but was not identified as the agency conducting these CERT-In trainings.
31.tq: Separate the agency responsible for training from the programme that supports research.

31.s: The National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems (NM-ICPS) supports research primarily in which area mentioned in the context of cybersecurity capacity building?
o: Universal acceptance of Indian language domains
Digital arrest investigation and victim restoration
31.x: NM-ICPS supports cybersecurity and artificial intelligence research.
31.tq: Application of the mission's stated research focus without confusing it with awareness campaigns or policing.

31.s: The Telangana Cyber Security Bureau's campaign titled “#OnlineButUnafraid” was aimed at which group?
o: Victims seeking restoration after digital arrest fraud
State police officers responsible for critical infrastructure
31.x: The Telangana Cyber Security Bureau launched the #OnlineButUnafraid campaign for women journalists.
31.tq: Direct recall of the campaign-name and target-group pairing.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the subject of the Supreme Court order referred to in the context of current cybercrime concerns?
o: Implementation of the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy
Ranking of countries in the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index
Training of IT professionals through ISEA
Digital-arrest standard operating procedures and restoration of victims' losses
31.x: The Supreme Court order concerned standard operating procedures for digital arrests and restoration of victims' losses.
31.tq: Identify the institutional subject matter rather than matching the issue with a similarly related cyber programme.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Cyber Security Policy 2013:
1. It had not been updated even by the time of the criticism referred to in the material.
2. Weak coordination was identified among CERT-In, the MHA portal and State police.
3. The criticism stated that coordination among these bodies was fully effective.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The 2013 policy was criticised for never having been updated, and coordination among CERT-In, the MHA portal and State police was described as weak. Statement 3 reverses that criticism.
31.tq: Use the negative statement carefully: the criticism concerned weak, not fully effective, coordination.

31.s: Which of the following correctly describes the implementation arrangement for the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy 2017?
o: It is implemented by APTS and includes four verticals.
It is implemented by NM-ICPS through two research pillars.
It is implemented by the MHA portal through three verticals.
It is implemented by CERT-In through five national pillars.
31.x: The Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy 2017 has four verticals and is implemented by APTS.
31.tq: Match the policy with its implementing agency and stated structural arrangement.

31.s: One of the verticals of the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy 2017 relates to:
o: Replacing the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index with a national rank
Administering the Supreme Court's digital-arrest SOPs
31.x: Securing critical government infrastructure is one of the four verticals of the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy 2017.
31.tq: Direct identification of a policy vertical from closely related cyber-governance functions.

31.s: Which of the following is another stated vertical of the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy 2017?
31.x: Capacity building is one of the four verticals of the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy 2017.
31.tq: Direct recall of the policy's capacity-building component.

31.s: In the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024, India was placed in which category, with what score?
o: Tier-1 (Role Modelling), with a score of 98.49
Tier-1 (Role Modelling), with a score of 88.49
31.x: India was placed in Tier-1, described as ‘Role Modelling’, and secured a score of 98.49 in the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024.
31.tq: Separate the category from the score and check both parts of the option.

31.s: Which organisation is associated with the Information Security Education and Awareness (ISEA) programme?
o: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
31.x: ISEA, or Information Security Education and Awareness, is associated with MeitY.
31.tq: Identify the correct ministry from the programme name and function.

31.s: Cyber Shakti is associated with training for which group?
31.x: Cyber Shakti is a programme for women government officials, with 305 participants at the beginner level and 53 at the advanced level.
31.tq: Identify the beneficiary group and avoid confusing it with other cyber programmes.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly states the participant figures associated with Cyber Shakti?
o: 305 total participants, with no advanced category
31.x: The stated Cyber Shakti figures are 305 beginner-level participants and 53 advanced-level participants.
31.tq: Watch for reversal of category-wise numerical data.

32.s: The right to privacy was declared to be intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21 in:
o: Gobind v. State of Madhya Pradesh
Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
32.x: In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, decided in 2017, the Supreme Court held that privacy is intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and protected under Part III.
32.tq: Identify the authoritative later case rather than the earlier cases that only raised or partially recognised privacy concerns.

32.s: The judgment in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India was delivered on:
32.x: The Puttaswamy privacy judgment was delivered on 24 August 2017.
32.tq: Distinguish the exact judgment date from nearby constitutional and subsequent privacy-law dates.

32.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the bench and conclusion in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India?
o: A nine-judge bench unanimously recognised privacy as intrinsic to life and personal liberty
A seven-judge bench unanimously held that privacy is outside Part III
A five-judge bench by a majority held that privacy is only a statutory right
A nine-judge bench held that privacy is available only to citizens
32.x: A unanimous nine-judge bench recognised privacy as intrinsic to life and personal liberty and protected under Article 21 and Part III.
32.tq: Check the bench strength, unanimity and constitutional status together.

32.s: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent that those decisions:
o: Recognised proportionality as the sole test for all restrictions
Denied the existence of privacy as a protected constitutional interest
Declared education to be a Directive Principle
32.x: Puttaswamy overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) insofar as they denied privacy as a constitutional protection.
32.tq: Focus on the limited extent of overruling instead of treating the earlier judgments as wholly erased.

32.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched in relation to the evolution of the right to privacy?
o: M.P. Sharma — 2017 recognition of privacy as intrinsic to Article 21
Kharak Singh — early concern relating to privacy
Gobind — denial that privacy forms part of liberty
Puttaswamy — privacy limited to a statutory entitlement
32.x: Kharak Singh represents an early concern relating to privacy. Gobind v. State of Madhya Pradesh in 1975 recognised privacy as part of liberty, while Puttaswamy gave privacy comprehensive constitutional protection.
32.tq: Use the chronological development of the doctrine to separate early concern, partial recognition and final constitutional affirmation.

32.s:
For an intrusion into the right to privacy to withstand constitutional scrutiny, which of the following requirements are relevant?
1. Legality, meaning the existence of a law.
2. A legitimate aim or need.
3. Proportionality.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: The privacy restriction framework includes legality, legitimate aim or need and proportionality. All three requirements are relevant to assessing an intrusion.
32.tq: Recognise the cumulative constitutional test instead of selecting only the most familiar element.

32.s: A government measure restricts personal data without any supporting law, although it claims to pursue a public objective. Which requirement of the privacy test is most clearly absent?
32.x: The legality requirement demands that an intrusion into privacy be supported by a law. A claimed public objective cannot substitute for the existence of legal authority.
32.tq: Apply the first step of the privacy test by asking whether the restriction has a legal basis.

32.s: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is associated with which institution?
32.x: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 provides for a Data Protection Board. The enacted law is an Act, not merely a Personal Data Protection Bill.
32.tq: Discriminate between the enacted statute and the earlier bill terminology, and identify its associated body.

32.s: The proportionality requirement in privacy jurisprudence was subsequently applied in the context of Aadhaar in:
32.x: The proportionality framework developed in privacy jurisprudence was subsequently applied to Aadhaar in 2018.
32.tq: Separate the year of the Puttaswamy judgment from the year of its later application to Aadhaar.

32.s: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) of the European Union was implemented from which date?
32.x: The EU GDPR, adopted in April 2016, was implemented from 25 May 2018.
32.tq: Use the precise implementation date rather than the adoption date.

32.s: Which of the following best describes the Right to Be Forgotten (RTBF)?
o: Removal, masking or de-indexing of outdated, irrelevant or harmful personal information
A right available only to government employees
Permanent deletion of every judicial record concerning a person
A right to prevent all forms of online identification
32.x: RTBF concerns the removal, masking or de-indexing of outdated, irrelevant or harmful personal information. It does not require the deletion of every judicial record.
32.tq: Identify the exact scope of the right instead of choosing an extreme formulation.

32.s: The Right to Be Forgotten originated in the European case of:
o: Laksh Vir Singh Yadav v Union of India
Kharak Singh v State of Uttar Pradesh
32.x: The RTBF originated in Google Spain v AEPD (2014).
32.tq: Match the right with the case in which it originated.

32.s: Under which provision of the GDPR was the Right to Be Forgotten formalised as the Right to Erasure?
32.x: The GDPR formalised the Right to Be Forgotten as the Right to Erasure under Article 17.
32.tq: Discriminate between closely related article and section numbers.

32.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Right to Be Forgotten from a general deletion of judicial records?
o: It applies only to biometric data collected by UIDAI.
It automatically cancels the judgment of a court.
It prohibits every search involving the person’s name.
It limits name-based searches without necessarily erasing judicial records.
32.x: The Indian understanding of RTBF does not erase judicial records; it can limit name-based searches in appropriate circumstances.
32.tq: Separate de-indexing or search limitation from destruction of the underlying record.

32.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Concept/Authority)
 a. DPDP Act, 2023
 b. GDPR
 c. Indian data subject terminology
 d. EU data subject terminology

List-II (Term)
 i. Data Controller
 ii. Data Fiduciary
 iii. Data Subject
 iv. Data Principal

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
32.x: The DPDP Act uses Data Fiduciary and Data Principal, while the GDPR uses Data Controller and Data Subject.
32.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes with reversed terminology.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the DPDP Act, 2023 and the GDPR:
1. The DPDP Act covers only digital personal data, whereas the GDPR covers all personal data.
2. The DPDP Act provides for financial penalties only, while the GDPR may involve financial and criminal penalties in some states.
3. Data portability is an explicit right under the GDPR but is not a statutory right under the DPDP Act.
4. Both frameworks use the term ‘Data Fiduciary’ for the entity determining the purposes of processing.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the GDPR uses ‘Data Controller’, whereas ‘Data Fiduciary’ is the DPDP Act terminology.
32.tq: Compare the frameworks row by row and detect the swapped legal term.

32.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched regarding cross-border data treatment?
o: DPDP Act — blacklist approach, subject to restrictions
DPDP Act — whitelist or adequacy approach only
GDPR — cross-border transfers linked with adequacy
32.x: The DPDP Act is described as following a blacklist approach, allowing transfers unless restricted. The whitelist or adequacy approach is associated with the GDPR.
32.tq: Find the reversed comparison in the cross-border transfer row.

32.s: Under the DPDP Act, 2023, the adjudicatory regulator is the:
o: Data Protection Authority of each State
32.x: The Data Protection Board of India is the adjudicatory regulator under the DPDP Act, 2023.
32.tq: Identify the exact statutory body instead of a similarly named authority.

32.s: Which statement correctly compares the regulators under the DPDP Act and the GDPR?
o: The DPDP Act provides for the Data Protection Board of India, while the GDPR operates through a Data Protection Authority in each member state.
The DPDP Act provides for one DPA in every member state, while the GDPR provides for one national Board in India.
Both frameworks provide for the same single regulator at the international level.
Neither framework provides an adjudicatory or regulatory authority.
32.x: The DPDP Act provides for the Data Protection Board of India, whereas the GDPR framework has a Data Protection Authority in each member state.
32.tq: Keep the institutional comparison aligned with the jurisdiction of each framework.

32.s: The maximum financial penalty specifically associated with the DPDP Act in the comparison of the two frameworks is:
32.x: The DPDP Act comparison specifies financial penalties of up to Rs 250 crore.
32.tq: Read the penalty figure precisely and reject altered magnitudes.

32.s: Which constitutional provision was used in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) to declare privacy a Fundamental Right?
32.x: The nine-judge Bench declared the Right to Privacy a Fundamental Right under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution. The judgment was also linked with Article 19 in the constitutional discussion.
32.tq: Identify the principal constitutional provision rather than a related procedural article.

32.s: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) was decided by:
o: A five-judge Bench by a majority of 4:1
32.x: The Puttaswamy privacy judgment was delivered by a unanimous nine-judge Bench on 24 August 2017.
32.tq: Distinguish the bench strength and voting pattern from the later Aadhaar judgment.

32.s: On which date was the nine-judge Puttaswamy privacy judgment delivered?
32.x: The unanimous nine-judge Puttaswamy judgment was delivered on 24 August 2017.
32.tq: Distinguish the Puttaswamy date from the Aadhaar judgment date.

32.s: The Puttaswamy judgment directed the government to:
32.x: The judgment directed the government to enact a data-protection law.
32.tq: Match the judgment with its institutional and legislative direction.

32.s: Which of the following cases were overruled by the Puttaswamy judgment to the extent that they denied privacy?
o: Aadhaar and Laksh Vir Singh Yadav
32.x: Puttaswamy overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) to the extent that those decisions denied a constitutional right to privacy.
32.tq: Use the paired-case association and distinguish it from cases recognising privacy concerns.

32.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Puttaswamy v Union of India
B. Gobind v State of Madhya Pradesh
C. Kharak Singh v State of Uttar Pradesh
D. M.P. Sharma v Satish Chandra
32.x: The correct sequence is M.P. Sharma (1954), Kharak Singh (1962), Gobind (1975), and Puttaswamy (2017).
32.tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two intervening cases by year.

32.s:
Match the following cases with the propositions associated with them:

List-I (Case)
 a. Kharak Singh v State of Uttar Pradesh
 b. Gobind v State of Madhya Pradesh
 c. Puttaswamy v Union of India

List-II (Proposition)
 i. Privacy recognised as part of personal liberty
 ii. Privacy recognised as a Fundamental Right and informational privacy affirmed
 iii. Early recognition of privacy concerns under Article 21

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
32.x: Kharak Singh is associated with early privacy concerns under Article 21; Gobind recognised privacy as part of personal liberty; Puttaswamy affirmed privacy as a Fundamental Right and informational privacy.
32.tq: Start with the distinctive Puttaswamy pair and then distinguish the two earlier recognitions.

32.s: The constitutional test for State intrusion into the right to privacy consists of:
32.x: The three-part test for State intrusion is legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
32.tq: Recall the three-part constitutional test as a complete sequence.

32.s: A State measure interferes with informational privacy. To satisfy the test associated with Puttaswamy, which combination must be examined?
o: Whether it is supported by a private contract alone
Whether it has legality, a legitimate aim and proportionality
Whether it affects only citizens and not residents
Whether it has parliamentary privilege, secrecy and permanence
32.x: State intrusion into privacy is tested through legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
32.tq: Apply the three-part test to a short constitutional scenario.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the Aadhaar judgment of 2018:
1. It was decided by a five-judge Bench.
2. The decision was by a majority of 4:1.
3. Justice D.Y. Chandrachud dissented.
4. The judgment was delivered on 26 September 2018.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: All four statements are correct: the Aadhaar judgment was delivered by a five-judge Bench on 26 September 2018 by 4:1, with Justice D.Y. Chandrachud dissenting.
32.tq: Combine bench strength, majority, dissent and date in one constitutional case cluster.

32.s: Which of the following was upheld in the Aadhaar judgment?
o: Section 57 permitting use by private entities without limitation
Mandatory Aadhaar linking with all bank accounts
Mandatory Aadhaar requirement for welfare benefits under Section 7
Mandatory linking of Aadhaar with mobile SIM cards
32.x: The Aadhaar Act was upheld, including mandatory Aadhaar for welfare benefits under Section 7. Mandatory linking with bank accounts and mobile SIMs was not upheld, and Section 57 relating to private entities was struck down.
32.tq: Distinguish upheld welfare use from the private and unrelated-linking provisions struck down or read down.

32.s: The Aadhaar judgment upheld Aadhaar-based linking for which of the following?
o: All mobile SIM connections as a general requirement
PAN and income-tax returns under Section 139AA of the Income-tax Act
32.x: The judgment upheld Aadhaar linking with PAN and income-tax returns under Section 139AA of the Income-tax Act.
32.tq: Identify the specific statutory linkage that was upheld among several broader claims.

32.s: Which one of the following was struck down or read down in the Aadhaar judgment?
o: The Aadhaar Act itself in its entirety
Section 57 concerning use by private entities
Section 139AA concerning PAN and income-tax returns
32.x: Section 57 of the Aadhaar Act, concerning use by private entities, was struck down. The Aadhaar Act was upheld, as were Section 7 welfare authentication and Section 139AA linkage.
32.tq: Find the provision belonging to the struck-down column rather than the upheld column.

32.s: The Aadhaar judgment did NOT uphold mandatory Aadhaar requirements relating to:
o: The Aadhaar Act and income-tax returns
Welfare benefits under Section 7 and PAN linking
Bank accounts, mobile SIMs, and specified educational examinations or admissions
32.x: Mandatory linking with bank accounts and mobile SIMs, as well as requirements relating to CBSE, NEET, UGC and school admissions, was struck down or not upheld.
32.tq: Group the provisions in the rejected category and watch for the EXCEPT-style reversal.

32.s: Which of the following was among the criticisms of the Aadhaar framework at the time of the 2018 judgment?
o: Lack of any provision for welfare authentication
Biometric data risks and absence of a data-protection law
32.x: The criticisms included risks associated with biometric data, the absence of a data-protection law, and mandatory linking requirements.
32.tq: Select the criticism that matches the privacy and data-protection concerns.

32.s: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was enacted in which year?
32.x: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was passed in August 2023.
32.tq: Direct year recall using nearby legislative milestones as distractors.

32.s: The President of India gave assent to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act on:
32.x: Presidential assent to the Act was given on 11 August 2023.
32.tq: Numerical date discrimination among closely related data-protection dates.

32.s:
With reference to the applicability of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, consider the following statements:
1. It applies to personal data processed digitally.
2. It applies to data collected digitally for subsequent digitisation.
3. It covers non-personal data.
4. It may cover entities outside India offering goods or services to persons in India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: The Act covers digitally processed or digitally collected data and certain entities outside India offering goods or services in India. It excludes non-personal data.
32.tq: Find the excluded category while testing territorial and functional scope.

32.s: Which expression is used in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act as a gender-neutral term for the individual whose personal data is processed?
32.x: A Data Principal is the individual whose personal data is processed, and the wording is gender-neutral.
32.tq: Distinguish closely related statutory terms by their exact roles.

32.s: In the case of a child below 18 years of age, who is treated as the Data Principal under the Digital Personal Data Protection framework?
32.x: For a child under 18, the parent or guardian is treated as the Data Principal.
32.tq: Apply a statutory definition to a short age-based scenario.

32.s: A person or entity deciding the purpose and means of processing personal data is known as the:
32.x: The Data Fiduciary determines the purpose and means of processing personal data.
32.tq: Role-definition recall with similar data-governance terms as distractors.

32.s: Which one of the following is NOT an additional obligation of a Significant Data Fiduciary?
o: Appointment of a Data Protection Officer in India
Automatic exemption from all consent requirements
32.x: A Significant Data Fiduciary must appoint a Data Protection Officer in India, appoint an independent auditor and undertake impact assessment. It does not receive an automatic exemption from consent requirements.
32.tq: Find the option that reverses an additional compliance duty into an exemption.

32.s: A Significant Data Fiduciary is notified by the Central Government primarily with reference to its:
32.x: Notification as a Significant Data Fiduciary is based on factors such as the volume and sensitivity of data, along with associated risks.
32.tq: Directly identify the statutory notification criteria rather than an unrelated corporate attribute.

32.s: Which of the following best describes a Consent Manager?
o: A government officer who investigates cybercrime
A registered entity through which a Data Principal gives, manages and withdraws consent
An auditor appointed only by a Significant Data Fiduciary
A tribunal hearing appeals from the Board
32.x: A Consent Manager is a registered entity enabling a Data Principal to give, manage and withdraw consent.
32.tq: Exact-term discrimination based on function and institutional role.

32.s: The Data Protection Board of India is best described as a/an:
o: Adjudicatory body set up by the Central Government
Appellate tribunal under the Reserve Bank of India
Advisory committee under the Planning Commission
Independent auditor appointed by a Data Fiduciary
32.x: The Data Protection Board of India is an adjudicatory body established by the Central Government.
32.tq: Identify the correct body by matching its nature and establishing authority.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Data Protection Board of India:
1. Its headquarters is in New Delhi.
2. Its members are appointed by the Central Government.
3. Appeals against its decisions lie to TDSAT.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: The Board is headquartered in New Delhi, its members are appointed by the Central Government, and appeals lie to TDSAT.
32.tq: Statement combination testing location, appointment and appellate authority.

32.s: The maximum penalty for failure to take reasonable security safeguards under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act is:
32.x: Failure of reasonable security safeguards may attract a maximum penalty of ₹250 crore.
32.tq: Numerical recall using the graded penalty figures as close distractors.

32.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding breaches and maximum penalties.

List-I (Breach)
a. Obligations regarding children's data
b. Additional duties of Significant Data Fiduciaries
c. Residual breach
d. Duties of Data Principals involving false information

List-II (Maximum penalty)
i. ₹10,000
ii. ₹50 crore
iii. ₹150 crore
iv. ₹200 crore

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
32.x: Children’s data obligations carry ₹200 crore, additional SDF duties ₹150 crore, residual breaches ₹50 crore and false information by Data Principals ₹10,000.
32.tq: Start from the sure penalty pair and eliminate codes with mismatched amounts.

32.s: Section 17 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act enables the Central Government to exempt state instrumentalities on grounds including:
o: Foreign investment and industrial licensing only
32.x: Section 17 permits exemptions for state instrumentalities on grounds such as sovereignty, security and public order.
32.tq: Recall the specific grounds while rejecting unrelated policy objectives.

32.s: Which of the following is an example of the type of activity for which a state instrumental­ity may be exempted from consent requirements under the stated exemption framework?
32.x: Law-enforcement activity such as biometric surveillance is cited as an example where consent may be exempted under the relevant government exemption.
32.tq: Apply the exemption to a public-security scenario rather than a commercial activity.

32.s: The final Digital Personal Data Protection Rules were notified on:
32.x: The final DPDP Rules were notified on 14 November 2025; 3 January 2025 was the date of release of the draft Rules.
32.tq: Distinguish the draft-release date from the final-notification date.

32.s: The draft Digital Personal Data Protection Rules were released on:
32.x: The draft Rules were released on 3 January 2025.
32.tq: Direct date recall with nearby Act and final-Rule dates as distractors.

32.s:
Arrange the following phases of implementation of the DPDP Rules in chronological order:
A. Full operational compliance
B. Establishment provisions of the Data Protection Board
C. Consent Manager provisions

Select the correct chronological sequence.
32.x: Board provisions came into force immediately in November 2025, Consent Manager provisions in November 2026 and full operational compliance in May 2027.
32.tq: Use the first and final implementation phases to order the middle phase.

32.s: The Consent Manager provisions under the DPDP Rules are scheduled to come into force in:
32.x: The Consent Manager provisions are scheduled for November 2026, twelve months after notification of the final Rules.
32.tq: Test the phased timetable through the exact month and interval.

32.s: Full operational compliance under the phased DPDP Rules is scheduled for:
32.x: Full operational compliance is scheduled for May 2027, eighteen months after the November 2025 notification.
32.tq: Identify the terminal phase rather than the immediate or intermediate phase.

32.s: Which one of the following is NOT among the fiduciary requirements highlighted in the DPDP Rules?
o: Unlimited retention of all collected data
32.x: The Rules require purpose limitation, data minimisation and retention controls. They do not permit unlimited retention of all collected data.
32.tq: Spot the option that reverses a data-governance principle.

32.s: Which set of practices is most consistent with the DPDP Rules?
o: Clear and specific consent, plain-language notices and purpose limitation
Consent without information, unrestricted collection and unlimited reuse
Implied consent, technical notices and indefinite retention
Anonymous consent, no retention controls and compulsory foreign storage
32.x: The Rules require clear, specific and informed consent, plain-language notices, purpose limitation, data minimisation and retention controls.
32.tq: Select the option containing the complete set of positive compliance practices.

32.s: Under the cross-border transfer approach in the DPDP Rules, personal data may generally be transferred:
o: To all countries except those restricted by the Government
Only to countries selected by the Reserve Bank of India
Only within India, without any exception
Only to countries specifically approved in a whitelist
32.x: The framework adopts a negative-list or blacklist approach: transfers are permitted except to countries restricted by the Government.
32.tq: Distinguish blacklist permission from whitelist permission.

32.s:
Arrange the following developments in the history of India’s personal-data protection legislation:
A. PDP Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha and referred to the JPC
B. DPDP Act passed and assent given
C. Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee drafted the 2018 Bill
D. PDP Bill withdrawn and a narrower DPDP draft released

Select the correct chronological sequence.
32.x: The sequence was 2017–18 Committee and draft, 2019 introduction and JPC reference, 2022 withdrawal and narrower draft, followed by the 2023 Act.
32.tq: Order the four legislative milestones by their stated years.

32.s: The Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee was constituted by which ministry in relation to the Personal Data Protection Bill?
o: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
32.x: The Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee was associated with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and drafted the Personal Data Protection Bill, 2018.
32.tq: Use the correct ministry-authority pairing and reject neighbouring ministries.

32.s: Which of the following correctly describes the 2021 report of the Joint Parliamentary Committee on the Personal Data Protection Bill?
o: It proposed 93 amendments and covered personal as well as non-personal data.
It withdrew the 2018 Bill and created the RBI payment-data mandate.
It notified the final DPDP Rules for 2025.
It proposed no amendments and dealt only with cloud computing.
32.x: The JPC report of 2021 proposed 93 amendments and covered both personal and non-personal data.
32.tq: Match the committee report with its year, amendment count and subject coverage.

32.s: The Personal Data Protection Bill was withdrawn in 2022 primarily in the context of:
o: The RBI’s decision to permit foreign storage of payment data
The completion of full DPDP compliance in May 2027
The abolition of the Data Protection Board
32.x: The Bill was withdrawn in 2022 citing compliance burden and ambiguity, after which a narrower DPDP draft was released.
32.tq: Identify the stated cause of withdrawal instead of confusing it with later implementation events.

32.s:
Match the following committees with their principal association.

List-I (Committee or group)
a. Justice A.P. Shah Group of Experts
b. Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee
c. Kris Gopalakrishnan Committee
d. A.K. Bhargava Committee

List-II (Association)
i. Non-personal data
 ii. Privacy
 iii. Personal Data Protection Bill
 iv. Net neutrality

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
32.x: The A.P. Shah Group dealt with privacy, the Srikrishna Committee with the Personal Data Protection Bill, the Kris Gopalakrishnan Committee with non-personal data and the A.K. Bhargava Committee with net neutrality.
32.tq: Start with the distinctive net-neutrality pairing and eliminate the remaining mismatches.

32.s: The Justice A.P. Shah Group of Experts on Privacy submitted its report in:
32.x: The Justice A.P. Shah Group of Experts on Privacy was associated with a 2012 report.
32.tq: Confusable-year discrimination between the privacy group and the later net-neutrality reference.

32.s: The Kris Gopalakrishnan Committee, associated with the year 2020, dealt with:
32.x: The Kris Gopalakrishnan Committee was constituted in 2020 in connection with non-personal data.
32.tq: Direct committee-subject matching with related committee subjects as distractors.

32.s: Which committee is associated with the 2015 net-neutrality reference mentioned in the legislative-history material?
o: A.K. Bhargava Committee of the Department of Telecommunications
32.x: The 2015 net-neutrality panel was the Department of Telecommunications’ A.K. Bhargava Committee, not the A.P. Shah privacy group.
32.tq: Discriminate between similarly cited committee names and subjects.

32.s: In April 2018, the Reserve Bank of India directed that:
o: Payment data should be transferred only to blacklisted countries
All payment-system data should be stored only in India
All personal data should be stored only outside India
Cloud-computing data should be stored only by the Central Government
32.x: The RBI’s April 2018 mandate required all payment-system data to be stored only in India.
32.tq: Direct mandate recall using authority and subject as the deciding clues.

32.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes the DPDP Act’s approach to cross-border data transfers from a whitelist model?
o: The Act permits transfers only to countries expressly approved by the RBI.
The Act requires every transfer to be approved by TDSAT.
The Act prohibits every transfer outside India.
The Act permits transfers except to countries restricted by the Central Government.
32.x: The DPDP Act uses a blacklist or negative-list approach, under which transfers are allowed unless the Central Government restricts particular countries.
32.tq: Test the reversed blacklist-versus-whitelist comparison.

32.s: India’s first national standards for Cloud Computing, Data Centres and Ethical AI focused on which combination of concerns?
o: Agricultural insurance, irrigation and food storage
Data sovereignty, algorithmic bias and privacy
Only payment settlement and monetary policy
Foreign exchange, tariffs and industrial licensing
32.x: The standards focused on data sovereignty, algorithmic bias and privacy and were aligned with the DPDP Act.
32.tq: Identify the complete thematic combination rather than a single isolated concern.

32.s: Which provision of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act amended Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act?
32.x: Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act amended Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act.
32.tq: Identify the exact statutory provision instead of confusing it with nearby sections.

32.s: The amendment to Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act enables public authorities to refuse disclosure of which category of information?
o: All information relating to public authorities
32.x: The amendment permits authorities to refuse all personal information, thereby removing the earlier public-interest override and the ‘no relationship to public activity’ test.
32.tq: Test the precise scope of the amended exemption rather than its general purpose.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the amendment to Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act:
1. The earlier public-interest override was removed.
2. The earlier test concerning absence of relationship to public activity was removed.
3. Personal information may be refused outright.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: All three statements are correct. Section 44(3) removed both the earlier public-interest override and the public-activity relationship test, allowing personal information to be refused outright.
32.tq: Check whether all three consequences flow from the same statutory amendment.

32.s:
With reference to litigation concerning the DPDP Act and the RTI Act, consider the following pairs:
1. Venkatesh Nayak — petition before a three-judge Bench headed by CJI Surya Kant
2. Constitution Bench — reference of challenges to the amendment
3. Geeta Seshu and SFLC — plea concerning personal data and public data
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
32.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. The litigation includes the Venkatesh Nayak petition, reference of challenges to a Constitution Bench, and the plea by Geeta Seshu and SFLC on personal data versus public data.
32.tq: Start with the sure person–litigation pair and verify the institutional details.

32.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. The Supreme Court asked whether the law was ‘crippling RTI’.
B. A three-judge Bench headed by CJI Surya Kant heard the Venkatesh Nayak petition.
C. Challenges were referred to a Constitution Bench.
D. The Supreme Court considered a plea concerning ‘personal data’ and ‘public data’ by Geeta Seshu and SFLC.
32.x: The sequence was 15 February 2026, 25 February 2026, 13 March 2026 and 8 August 2026 respectively.
32.tq: Use the dates to fix the first and last events before ordering the middle events.

32.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched with the DPDP Act’s exemptions or exclusions?
o: Notified State agencies — possible exemption on grounds of sovereignty, security or public order
32.x: Journalism receives no exemption. Notified State agencies, research, archiving, statistics and potentially startups are the categories referred to for exemptions.
32.tq: Find the exception by distinguishing a possible exemption from the expressly excluded category.

32.s: Which provision of the DPDP Act permits the State to process personal data without obtaining consent in specified circumstances?
32.x: Section 7, dealing with ‘legitimate uses’, allows the State to process data without consent.
32.tq: Match the statutory section with the function it performs.

32.s: The Supreme Court-appointed technical committee in the Pegasus matter was supervised by:
32.x: The technical committee was supervised by Justice R.V. Raveendran.
32.tq: Apply the wrong-person trap to distinguish the supervising judge from other judicial figures.

32.s: Which of the following correctly describes the finding of the Supreme Court-appointed technical committee in the Pegasus matter?
o: Malware was found on five of 29 phones, but it could not be conclusively linked to Pegasus.
The committee conclusively established that Pegasus had been used by a particular government agency.
Pegasus was conclusively found on all 29 phones examined.
No malware was found on any of the phones examined.
32.x: The committee found malware on five of the 29 phones examined, but could not conclusively establish that it was Pegasus.
32.tq: Separate the numerical finding from the stronger but unsupported claim of conclusive attribution.

32.s: Which of the following legal combinations is associated with interception of communications in India?
o: Section 69 of the IT Act and Section 5(2) of the Telegraph Act, now under the Telecommunications Act, 2023
Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act and Section 17 of the DPDP Act
Section 7 of the DPDP Act and the Constitution Bench procedure
The GDPR and the Telecommunications Act, 1885
32.x: Interception is associated with Section 69 of the IT Act and Section 5(2) of the Telegraph Act, 1885, with the latter framework now under the Telecommunications Act, 2023.
32.tq: Match each interception provision with its correct statute and legislative successor.

32.s: The safeguards governing interception, referred to in the context of privacy protection, were laid down in:
o: Laksh Vir Singh Yadav v Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
Puttaswamy v Union of India, 2017 only
32.x: The relevant safeguards for interception were laid down in PUCL v Union of India in 1997.
32.tq: Use the case-name and year pair to avoid confusing interception safeguards with broader privacy judgments.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding facial-recognition surveillance:
1. A Member of Parliament approached the Supreme Court against the Delhi Police’s use of facial-recognition technology during NEET-UG protests.
2. The National Automated Facial Recognition System operates without a specific statute.
3. State surveillance must satisfy the tests laid down in Puttaswamy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: All three statements are correct. The challenge concerned Delhi Police use during NEET-UG protests, NAFRS operates without a statute, and surveillance must meet the Puttaswamy tests.
32.tq: Check each statement independently, especially the statutory-status statement containing ‘without’.

32.s: Which of the following is NOT a recognised right of a Data Principal under the DPDP framework?
o: Right to impose criminal penalties on a Data Fiduciary
32.x: The listed rights include information and access, correction, erasure, grievance redress, withdrawal of consent and nomination. A Data Principal does not impose criminal penalties on a Data Fiduciary.
32.tq: Identify the outsider by separating an individual data right from an enforcement power.

32.s: Which of the following is a duty of a Data Principal?
o: To avoid furnishing false information or impersonating another person
To appoint the Data Protection Board
To exempt startups from the DPDP Act
To provide only verified parental consent for every adult’s data
32.x: A Data Principal must not provide false information or impersonate another person. Avoiding frivolous complaints is another stated duty.
32.tq: Translate the statutory duty into a practical conduct-based situation.

32.s: In relation to processing the personal data of children, which one of the following is correct?
o: Verifiable parental consent is required for persons below 18 years of age.
Consent is required only for targeted advertisements, not for processing data.
Only written consent from the school is required.
Parental consent is unnecessary if the child is above 16 years of age.
32.x: The framework requires verifiable parental consent for persons under 18 years of age.
32.tq: Use the age threshold to distinguish children’s-data consent from adult consent.

32.s: Which of the following activities is prohibited when aimed at children under the DPDP framework?
o: Processing under legitimate uses by the State
Tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising
32.x: Tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertisements aimed at children are prohibited.
32.tq: Find the prohibited conduct by grouping the child-protection restrictions together.

32.s: The penalty mentioned for a breach relating to children’s data is up to:
32.x: A breach relating to children’s data may attract a penalty of up to ₹200 crore.
32.tq: Compare the numerical penalty with the separate ₹10,000 duty-related penalty.

32.s: In Laksh Vir Singh Yadav v Union of India, the Delhi High Court dealt with which issue?
o: Interception under Section 69 of the IT Act
Exemption of startups from data protection obligations
De-indexing name-based search results for acquitted persons
Appointment of the Data Protection Board
32.x: The Delhi High Court laid down a framework for de-indexing name-based results concerning persons who had been acquitted.
32.tq: Match the case with its distinctive remedy rather than with a general privacy principle.

32.s: The rules relating to Consent Managers were expected by which month and year?
32.x: Consent Manager rules were due in November 2026.
32.tq: Read the deadline precisely and distinguish it from the publication date of the forecast.

32.s:
Consider the following criticisms and debates concerning the DPDP framework:
1. Broad exemptions for the State
2. Absence of data portability
3. Questions concerning Board independence
4. Dilution of RTI through Section 44(3)
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: All four are identified criticisms or areas of debate concerning the DPDP framework.
32.tq: Test a complete list by checking whether the final item is also included rather than stopping at the familiar first three.

32.s: The AP Police AI4AP pilot referred to in the context of DPDP compliance is being undertaken in which districts?
32.x: The AI4AP pilot is associated with Chittoor, Guntur and Annamayya, and raises DPDP compliance issues.
32.tq: Use the location-list distinction to identify the exact districts involved in the pilot.

32.s: Which of the following is linked to the DPDP Act in the context of current national standards?
o: Standards on cloud, data centres and ethical artificial intelligence
Standards only on agricultural markets and crop insurance
32.x: National standards on cloud services, data centres and ethical AI are linked to the DPDP Act.
32.tq: Connect the broad technology-governance domains with the data-protection framework.

32.s: Which statement best describes the comparative position of the DPDP framework vis-à-vis the GDPR?
o: The DPDP framework is broader, more detailed and primarily criminal-penalty based.
The DPDP framework is narrower, lighter and based on financial penalties.
The DPDP framework excludes all financial penalties and relies only on data portability.
The two frameworks are identical in scope and enforcement.
32.x: The DPDP framework is described as narrower and lighter than the GDPR, with a financial-penalty-based enforcement approach.
32.tq: Test all three comparison dimensions—scope, regulatory weight and penalty model—together.

32.s: Which of the following issues is specifically included among the debates concerning journalists and the DPDP framework?
o: Journalists being treated as Data Fiduciaries
Journalists being made members of the Consent Manager authority
Journalists being prohibited from filing RTI applications
Journalists receiving an automatic exemption from all obligations
32.x: The debates include the treatment of journalists as ‘Data Fiduciaries’; journalism does not receive a general exemption.
32.tq: Distinguish the debated classification of journalists from the separate question of exemption.

32.s: Which of the following correctly identifies the status of the Supreme Court’s DPDP–RTI proceedings mentioned for August 2026?
o: The challenge concerned only children’s targeted advertising.
The Supreme Court had dismissed the challenge without examination.
The matter had been transferred exclusively to the Delhi High Court.
The Supreme Court was hearing the challenge concerning the DPDP Act and RTI.
32.x: The Supreme Court was hearing the challenge to the interaction between the DPDP Act and the RTI framework in August 2026.
32.tq: Distinguish an ongoing hearing from a final judicial determination.

32.s: The Data Protection Board of India has been created under which legislation?
32.x: The Data Protection Board of India was created under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
32.tq: Test the parent legislation of the statutory body.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Data Protection Board of India:
1. It is an independent adjudicatory body.
2. It consists of four members.
3. It has an online complaints portal under the DPDP Rules, 2025.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
